_meta.what: The names lexicon of scripts/check_no_names.py's prose check (v1.291.0): real people our own written text has named. The owner's rule (U203 a, 17 Nov 2026): a name stays only where the name is the thing itself. The gate refuses every entry in authored prose, in a flashcard, in a clip title and in a credit line, outside the allowed kinds it names.
_meta.matching: `full_names` and `phrases`: whole words, case ignored, any run of spaces between the words. `single_tokens` (a surname, a first name or a nickname our text used alone) and the DERIVED SURNAMES (the last word of every full name, computed by the gate, never listed here): whole word, CASE-SENSITIVE, so the surname 'Hall' is not the word 'hall'.
_meta.people_only: `full_names` and `single_tokens` hold PEOPLE: the gate refuses an entry that does not parse as a person's name (two to five capitalised words for a full name, one for a token, and none of the words that mark a gym, a team or a channel). A phrase that names a person through a technique's own word goes to `phrases`, with its reason.
_meta.surnames_not_held: A derived surname is NOT held when it is (1) a word of one of the graph's own names or aliases, (2) listed in `technique_words`, or (3) listed in `ordinary_surnames` with its reason. The gate prints all three sets every run. `ordinary_surnames` has a cap in the script: a surname moves there by hand.
_meta.rule: Add a person when our text names one, and raise LEXICON_FLOOR in the script to the count the gate prints, in the same change. NEVER add a word a technique or position is named by: the gate refuses a token that is a whole word of a graph name or alias, or that is listed in `technique_words`.
_meta.allowed_rows: `origin_lines` (U206 a: who the technique of THAT record is named after, and nobody else), `citations` (the in-text citation of a Learning page's own listed reference) and `guide_titles` (a sentence in which a Systems guide's own title stands). Each row is ONE PLACE: a record, a field and the exact sentence, allowed once there. `names` is what the lexicon finds in the sentence; the gate refuses a row the lexicon no longer agrees with. The same sentence in any other field or record is a finding. Each list has a cap in the script (ALLOWED_CAPS): a new row is a ruling, and the cap moves by hand with it.

origin_lines.sentence: Popularized by Joe D'Arce and refined across modern no-gi competition, this front-headlock control sits at the intersection of the arm triangle and anaconda choke families.

Developed by Ricardo De La Riva in the 1980s as a counter to the traditional standing guard pass, this position revolutionized modern guard play by introducing a systematic approach to controlling the opponent's base from an off-angle relationship.

Named after Ricardo De La Riva who revolutionized its use in the 1980s, this position is characterized by the bottom player hooking their opponent's leg from the outside while controlling the opposite sleeve or collar.

Dead Orchard Control is Nathan Orchard's high rubber-guard trap in which the bottom player triangles the legs around the opponent's shoulders with both arms inside, creating short arm-lock opportunities.

origin_lines.sentence: The Single Leg X to Estima Lock is one of the most direct and reliable entries into the inverted footlock made famous by the Estima brothers, exploiting the foot control that Single Leg X-Guard already grants.

Named after Tarik Hopstock, this technique exploits the trapped arm configuration of Meathook by threading the bottom player's leg over the opponent's shoulder into a modified omoplata position while simultaneously securing a wrist grip that adds rotational torque to the shoulder attack.

The Kimura is one of the most versatile and high-percentage shoulder locks in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, named after judoka Masahiko Kimura who famously used it in a 1951 victory.

The Mir Lock is a straight-arm shoulder lock applied from top control that drives an isolated arm into shoulder hyperextension and external rotation using body weight, named after Frank Mir's UFC 48 finish.

The name pays homage to UFC Hall of Famer Frank Mir, who at UFC 48 secured a kimura grip on the opponent and finished with a straight armlock that snapped the forearm — a true arm/elbow break rather than a shoulder break, so the namesake honors Mir's signature figure-four arm control rather than this specific shoulder-hyperextension finish.
